summary: Defines the Datagram Congestion Control Protocol, a transport protocol offering two-way unicast connections of congestion-controlled but unreliable datagrams. It suits applications that move fairly large amounts of data and want control over the tradeoff between timeliness and reliability. It is standards-track and was later updated by RFC 5595, RFC 5596, RFC 6335, and RFC 6773.

plainLanguage.summary: DCCP (Datagram Congestion Control Protocol) lets programs send messages quickly while still slowing down when the network is congested. Unlike TCP, it does not resend lost messages, so it suits live applications where old data is useless.

subtitle: A congestion-controlled but unreliable transport for timely datagram delivery

tldr.problem: Applications like streaming need timely delivery without arbitrary delays from reliability; UDP lacks congestion control and TCP can delay data arbitrarily.
tldr.mechanism: DCCP establishes a connection, negotiates congestion control (CCID), and acknowledges packets so senders respond to loss and ECN marks, but never retransmits lost data.
tldr.outcome: Provides congestion-controlled, unreliable datagram flows with ECN support and a choice of congestion behavior; updated by RFC 5595, RFC 5596, RFC 6335, and RFC 6773.

today: RFC 4340 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted, but it has been updated by RFC 5595, RFC 5596, RFC 6335, and RFC 6773. Congestion control details are in RFC 4341 and RFC 4342.

sections.title: What DCCP Provides and Why
sections.content:
The Datagram Congestion Control Protocol (DCCP) is a transport protocol for bidirectional, unicast connections of congestion-controlled, unreliable datagrams. It is designed for applications that move fairly large amounts of data and want control over the tradeoff between timeliness and reliability, such as streaming media.

DCCP sits between UDP and TCP. TCP gives reliable in-order delivery, but that and its congestion control can cause arbitrarily long delays. UDP avoids long delays, but any UDP application that needs congestion control must build it itself. DCCP provides congestion control, including support for Explicit Congestion Notification (ECN), without the arbitrary delays from retransmission.

DCCP offers unreliable datagram flows, reliable handshakes for setup and teardown, reliable negotiation of options, mechanisms to avoid holding state for unacknowledged connection attempts, acknowledgements that report loss and ECN information, and Path MTU discovery. It is described as TCP minus bytestream semantics and reliability, or as UDP plus congestion control, handshakes, and acknowledgements.
sections.plainLanguage: Some programs, like video streams, care more about speed than getting every piece. DCCP lets them send messages quickly while still being polite about not overloading the network.

sections.title: Packets and the Generic Header
sections.content:
Every DCCP packet starts with a fixed-size generic header, followed by extra fixed fields depending on packet type, then options, then application data. The DCCP header is from 12 to 1020 bytes long.

The generic header carries source and destination ports, a Data Offset, a 4-bit CCVal for the sender's congestion control mechanism, a 4-bit Checksum Coverage field, a 16-bit checksum, a 4-bit Type, and the sequence number. The X bit selects the form: when X=1, the sequence number is 48 bits and the header is 16 bytes; when X=0, only the low 24 bits are sent and the header is 12 bytes.

Ten packet types are defined. A connection begins with DCCP-Request and DCCP-Response, carries data in DCCP-Data, DCCP-Ack, and DCCP-DataAck, and ends with DCCP-CloseReq, DCCP-Close, and DCCP-Reset. DCCP-Sync and DCCP-SyncAck resynchronize endpoints after bursts of loss. All packets except DCCP-Request and DCCP-Data carry an Acknowledgement Number.
sections.plainLanguage: Every DCCP packet starts with a label saying where it came from, where it is going, what kind it is, and its place in line. This lets both sides keep track of messages without resending lost ones.

sections.title: Feature Negotiation
sections.content:
A DCCP feature is a connection attribute on whose value both endpoints agree. Each feature applies to each endpoint separately, so client and server can have different values. Features include which congestion control mechanism (CCID) each direction uses.

Agreement uses four options: Change L, Confirm L, Change R, and Confirm R. L options come from the endpoint where the feature lives; R options come from the other endpoint. A Change starts negotiation and is retransmitted until a response arrives; a Confirm completes it.

Two reconciliation rules apply. With server-priority, each side lists values in preference order and the result is the first entry in the server's list that also appears in the client's list. With non-negotiable, the feature location announces a value and the other side must accept any valid value.

Features 1-9 are defined in the RFC (including Congestion Control ID, ECN Incapable, Ack Ratio, and Send Ack Vector). Features 128-255 are reserved for CCID-specific use. The Mandatory option marks the following option as required; if not understood, the receiver MUST reset with Reset Code 6.
sections.plainLanguage: Before exchanging data, the two computers agree on settings like how they will respond to congestion. They keep asking until both sides confirm the agreement.

sections.title: Opening, Running, and Closing a Connection
sections.content:
Setup uses a three-way handshake. The client sends DCCP-Request carrying a 32-bit Service Code naming the application-level service. The server answers with DCCP-Response, and the client replies with DCCP-Ack or DCCP-DataAck. To avoid holding state for unacknowledged attempts, the server may put its handshake state in an opaque Init Cookie option for the client to echo back.

Closing is also a handshake. A server that does not want to hold TIMEWAIT state sends DCCP-CloseReq; the client answers DCCP-Close; the server answers DCCP-Reset with Reset Code 1 (Closed). Either side may send DCCP-Close directly. Whoever receives the DCCP-Reset holds TIMEWAIT for 2MSL (4 minutes). Every DCCP connection ends with a DCCP-Reset, and the Reset Code indicates whether the close was clean.

Unlike TCP, DCCP has no receive window in the same sense, no simultaneous open, and no half-closed states.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a phone call: dial, pick up and say hello, hello back. Hanging up takes a short exchange, and one side waits briefly to avoid confusing a later call.

sections.title: Sequence Numbers and Acknowledgements
sections.content:
DCCP sequence numbers count packets, not bytes. Every packet increments the number by one; even repeated handshake packets get new sequence numbers. Arithmetic is modulo 2^48. This lets endpoints detect network duplicates and lost acknowledgements.

Since nothing is retransmitted, DCCP does not use cumulative byte acknowledgements. The Acknowledgement Number holds the greatest sequence number received on an acknowledgeable packet; options like the Ack Vector indicate which packets in between were received or missed.

Each endpoint keeps a sequence-validity window set by the Sequence Window feature (initial 100, minimum 32). Packets outside the window are sequence-invalid and elicit a DCCP-Sync; implementations SHOULD rate-limit Syncs (e.g., at most eight per second). DCCP-Sync and DCCP-SyncAck resynchronize after bursts of loss.

DCCP tracks maximum packet size from Path MTU discovery. Senders should send unfragmentable packets; DCCP-Sync packets padded to size can serve as safe probes.
sections.plainLanguage: Every packet gets its own number, even the ones that just say thanks. If something is missing, the other side knows exactly which packet was lost; nobody tries to resend it.

sections.title: Congestion Control and ECN
sections.content:
Congestion control is chosen by a one-byte CCID (Congestion Control Identifier), negotiated via feature 1. Each direction uses its own CCID; new connections start with CCID 2. Two CCIDs are defined: CCID 2 (RFC 4341) is TCP-like, and CCID 3 (RFC 4342) is TCP-Friendly Rate Control (TFRC). CCID 2 halves the congestion window on congestion events and typically sends one acknowledgement per two packets; CCID 3 is equation-based and smoother, sending acknowledgements roughly once per round-trip time.

DCCP is fully ECN-aware. Senders SHOULD mark packets as ECN-capable unless the receiver's ECN Incapable feature is set. To detect receivers that hide congestion, senders use ECN Nonces: they randomly pick between two ECN code points and acknowledgements echo the parity; mismatches can trigger an aggression penalty.

The Slow Receiver option indicates the receiver is struggling; the sender SHOULD NOT increase its rate for about one round-trip time. It is not a congestion signal.
sections.plainLanguage: When the network is crowded, everyone slows down. DCCP lets each program pick a style: stop-and-go like TCP, or a steady, smooth speed like TFRC.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
DCCP does not provide cryptographic security. Applications needing integrity, authentication, confidentiality, or access control should use IPsec or other end-to-end security.

Against off-path attackers (who cannot see traffic), DCCP uses mechanisms to limit hijacking and denial of service: initial sequence numbers must be chosen well, the Init Cookie option avoids state for unacknowledged requests, rate limits apply to DCCP-Sync and other responses, and options that could cause resets are handled carefully. The Data Dropped option lets receivers report why a packet was dropped without treating all loss as congestion.

Middleboxes should not assume port numbers alone identify applications (the Service Code in DCCP-Request provides service identification), and should be careful with partial checksums because uncovered data may change in transit. Unknown options MUST be ignored rather than causing resets except when marked Mandatory.
sections.plainLanguage: DCCP helps prevent certain attacks from outsiders who cannot see traffic, but it does not encrypt messages. If you need to keep secrets, add encryption yourself.
